existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Higginbotham develops race as a metalanguage shaping gender, class and sexuality and as a contested instrument of power. Her opening programme combines feminist theory with Black intellectual traditions; no single undifferentiated school affiliation. The target is the named strand, displayed under its parent entry.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham explicitly uses Scott’s infrapolitics for her discussion of micropolitical resistance (1992).
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Her note 67 identifies Domination and the Arts of Resistance, pp183–192; James C. Scott is distinct from Joan W. Scott.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham credits Hine’s reading, suggestions and questions on an earlier version of her 1992 article.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: This is a named draft-feedback contribution, not evidence that Hine originated the article’s theory.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham adapts Foucault’s technologies terminology to race, gender and sexuality (1992).
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Her p. 252 n4 names History of Sexuality1 and explains the term alongside Teresa de Lauretis; neither resource is exclusive.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham places Scott’s language-and-discourse turn among feminist frameworks she found compelling but insufficiently attentive to race.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Her 2017 retrospective, printed p.632, names Scott’s 1986 article and 1988 book before explaining her qualified dissatisfaction with feminist theory’s racial presumptions. The criticism concerns a wider body of theory, with Scott a named example, not Scott alone. This is Higginbotham’s retrospective account of the context of her 1992 intervention, not evidence of a private exchange, a 1992 direct denunciation or rejection of every Scott argument. James C.Scott’s separate infrapolitics resource is a different person.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham recalls that her father’s devotion to Woodson’s historical mission led her into history, a commitment she later deepened through reading Woodson.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own oral-history testimony, 16 June 2011, transcribed by Ashley Robertson in the 2012 NPS study, printed 185 and 188. Albert N. D. Brooks is the essential intermediary; this does not make Woodson her personal academic supervisor. Higginbotham also identifies insufficient attention to African American women in the earlier scholars’ groundwork at 188; admiration does not erase that qualification. Her father’s recollections, her childhood visits and her later reading remain distinct. Only selected transcript passages were read; no interview recording or full monograph reading is claimed.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Bederman credits Higginbotham’s analysis of race and gender among recent theoretical discussions informing the intersection she investigates.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: At5 Bederman explicitly adopts Hazel Carby’s call to interrogate racial specificity and whiteness. Note23 also identifies Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, together with Berger/Brown/Hewitt and Lerner, as important recent theoretical discussions. This plural, bounded historiographic resource does not replace the more direct Carby credit or imply exclusive derivation. Higginbotham original unread; no guessed correction of the date as printed in Bederman’s note.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Cites Higginbotham’s analysis of race alongside Fields when arguing for historically specific studies of racial practices.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Sugrue 393 makes Fields’s construction argument the explicit starting point and n7 adds Higginbotham’s African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race, continuing onto 394. This establishes a specific supporting resource, not a transfer of Fields’s primary credit to Higginbotham or proof of full agreement. The original article remains unread; neither an editorial tribute nor a citation-chain inference supplies the relationship.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Kerber expressly credits Higginbotham’s interpretation of race as a resource for her discussion of Black women and the separate-spheres framework.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 1988 printed26/n30 acknowledges an interpretive debt to Evelyn Brooks, The Problem of Race in Women’s History, alongside separately credited work by the Hortons, Sterling, Jones and Deborah Gray White. Higginbotham’s own Harvard CV establishes the identity through that distinctive chapter title and editor; metadata does not itself establish the debt. Kerber’s forthcoming volume title is preserved, not silently replaced with the later 1989 title. Printed9 also thanks Evelyn Brooks for counsel on earlier drafts, among many colleagues; no individual task or final chapter edition is inferred. Higginbotham chapter itself unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Hine uses Higginbotham’s account of churches as safe spaces to support her explanation of Black institutions that nurtured political discussion and resistance under segregation.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own Briggs 1066/n48 explicitly points to Righteous Discontent (1993), 10 for the church’s safe-space role. This particular historical resource supports Hine’s account of parallel institutions, not full adoption of every claim about respectability or proof of personal training. Kevin Gaines’s 1997 review is separately cited in the same note and is not erased. Original book/review unread; 1989 n9 earlier Burroughs chapter separately held with identity/source limits.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Higginbotham explicitly uses Hine’s culture of dissemblance to explain Black women’s protective silence about sexuality and the political significance of their self-representation.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Recipient’s own 1992 printed 266/n44 names and develops Hine’s argument, particularly for middle-class women, within a discussion of racialized sexuality and double-voiced discourse. This conceptual resource differs from existing 1622 Hine’s named draft feedback on 251. Higginbotham 272–273 also addresses costs of respectability/silencing; resource use does not mean complete agreement or that Hine originated every component of Higginbotham’s framework. Original cited Hine 1989 freshly checked; other cited scholars unread.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: White contributes a history of enslaved women; Higginbotham’s 1992 opening challenges thin racial analysis while developing feminist accounts of power. Distinct interventions, not a claim that one theorist founded intersectional inquiry.

named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her 1992 opening credits conceptual advances and cites Scott, Butler and others while challenging their racial limits. This later exchange does not explain the origins of Black historiography.
